quiz.explain: La Communauté a été fondée à Lisbonne en 1996.

quiz.q: Quel pays a rejoint la CPLP en 2014 après avoir fait du portugais une langue officielle ?
quiz.explain: Ancienne colonie espagnole au passé portugais à Annobón.

quiz.q: Quel pays lusophone est membre du Commonwealth ?
quiz.explain: Il l'a rejoint en 1995.

quiz.q: Quelles sont les deux langues officielles du Timor-Leste ?
quiz.explain: Le tétoum est la principale langue du quotidien.

quiz.q: Quel État américain abrite les communautés portugaises de Fall River et New Bedford ?
quiz.explain: Des baleiniers açoriens s'y installèrent au XIXe siècle.

lessons.title: Le Portugal au XXe siècle
lessons.summary: Dictature, guerres coloniales, révolution et Europe.

cards.title: La vie sous l'Estado Novo
cards.text: Le régime de Salazar reposait sur « Dieu, Patrie, Famille ». Il censurait la presse, interdisait partis et grèves, employait la police politique PIDE, et maintenait le Portugal pauvre et largement rural, avec une forte émigration.

deep.x: António de Oliveira Salazar, an economics professor, became finance minister in 1928 and prime minister in 1932. His 1933 constitution created the **Estado Novo** ("New State"), which lasted until 1974, one of Europe's longest dictatorships.
How control worked

x: Censors with the famous "blue pencil" cut newspapers, books, films and songs
The PIDE political police used informers, torture and the Tarrafal prison camp in Cape Verde
Elections were held, but the opposition was harassed and the results managed
Strikes were illegal; workers and bosses were organised in state "corporations"

deep.x: A poor country

Salazar balanced the budget and kept Portugal out of the Second World War, but he distrusted industry and mass education. Most people lived from small farms; many homes had no electricity or running water.
Women's lives were tightly limited: a married woman needed her husband's permission for some jobs and to travel abroad, and nurses and air hostesses long faced marriage restrictions.
The Estado Novo bought stability with silence: no free press, no free parties and very little change.
Opponents later summed up the regime's popular culture as the "three Fs": Fado, Fátima and Futebol.

cards.title: Émigration
cards.text: Des années 1950 aux années 1970, bien plus d'un million de Portugais ont émigré, beaucoup clandestinement (« a salto ») vers la France, l'Allemagne et le Luxembourg, fuyant la pauvreté et le service militaire.

deep.x: Portugal had always sent people abroad, mostly to Brazil. After about 1960 the flow turned to Europe, where France and West Germany were booming and short of workers. Between 1960 and 1974 roughly 1.5 million Portuguese left, out of a population of under 9 million.
Leaving "a salto"

The state limited legal emigration, so many people went clandestinely. They paid smugglers ("passadores") to guide them on foot over the mountains into Spain and across the Pyrenees into France. Young men also fled to avoid being sent to fight in Africa.
Life abroad

Many first lived in shanty towns, such as the bidonville at Champigny-sur-Marne near Paris, and worked in construction, factories and cleaning. They sent money home, and built houses in their villages that you can still spot today.
Emigration was the Portuguese people's own way out of poverty and war when the regime offered neither.
Every August, emigrants returning home on holiday became so visible that the month's festivals in northern villages still revolve around "os emigrantes".

cards.title: Les guerres coloniales

events.l: début de la guerre en Angola

cards.text: À partir de 1961, le Portugal combattit des mouvements indépendantistes en Angola, en Guinée-Bissau et au Mozambique. En 13 ans, environ 800 000 Portugais ont servi ; environ 9 000 sont morts, ainsi que bien plus d'Africains.

deep.x: While Britain and France were giving up their African colonies, Salazar insisted that Angola, Mozambique and Guinea were "overseas provinces" of one nation "from Minho to Timor". Independence movements, blocked from peaceful change, took up arms.
Three fronts

Guinea was the hardest front: by the early 1970s the PAIGC controlled much of the countryside. Fighting was mostly guerrilla war: ambushes, mines and raids, with napalm and forced resettlement of villagers on the Portuguese side. Massacres such as Wiriyamu in Mozambique (1972) were exposed abroad.
The cost

Conscripts served up to four years. Tens of thousands came back wounded or with lasting trauma, long rarely discussed. African deaths, among fighters and civilians, were far higher, though exact numbers are uncertain.
The colonial wars drained Portugal's money and young men, and the soldiers who fought them ended up overthrowing the regime.

deep.w: The wars were far away and barely touched daily life
deep.r: Almost every family had a son, brother or husband in Africa

cards.title: Humberto Delgado

events.l: assassiné par la PIDE en Espagne

cards.text: À l'élection présidentielle de 1958, le général Humberto Delgado défia le régime. Interrogé sur ce qu'il ferait de Salazar, il répondit : « Obviamente, demito-o ! » (« Évidemment, je le limoge ! »). Il perdit un scrutin truqué et fut assassiné par la PIDE en 1965.

deep.x: Humberto Delgado was an air force general who had served the regime loyally. He had lived in the USA and Canada and came back convinced that Portugal needed democracy. In 1958 he stood for president against the regime's candidate, Admiral Américo Tomás.
"Obviously, I'll sack him"

At a press conference in Lisbon's Café Chave d'Ouro on 10 May 1958, a journalist asked what he would do with Salazar if elected. His answer, "Obviamente, demito-o!", electrified the country. Huge crowds greeted him in Porto and Lisbon, and police charged the crowds.
Fraud and exile

The official result gave Delgado about a quarter of the vote. Most historians think the real result was much closer, but there was no free count. Afterwards the regime ended direct presidential elections. Delgado sought asylum in the Brazilian embassy and went into exile.
The murder

In February 1965 PIDE agents lured him to the Spanish border near Badajoz, pretending to be opposition contacts. They killed him and his Brazilian secretary, Arajaryr Campos. Their bodies were found weeks later.
One sentence from a general showed that the regime's support was far thinner than it claimed.
Lisbon's airport has been officially named Aeroporto Humberto Delgado since 2016.

cards.title: De Salazar à Caetano
cards.text: Salazar fut frappé d'incapacité en 1968 après une chute et remplacé par Marcelo Caetano, qui promit des réformes mais conserva les guerres coloniales et le cœur du régime.

deep.x: In August 1968 Salazar, then 79, fell from a deckchair at his summer residence in Estoril and later suffered a brain haemorrhage. President Américo Tomás replaced him in September with Marcelo Caetano, a law professor and long-time regime insider.
The "Marcelist Spring"

Caetano's motto was "evolution in continuity". Censorship was eased a little, the PIDE was renamed DGS, some exiles such as Mário Soares were allowed back for a time, and the economy grew. A "liberal wing" of young deputies, including Francisco Sá Carneiro, entered parliament hoping to reform from inside.
Spring turns to winter

x: The wars went on and costs kept rising
The liberal deputies resigned in frustration by 1973
The 1973 oil shock hit prices hard
In February 1974 General António de Spínola published "Portugal e o Futuro", arguing the wars could not be won militarily

deep.x: Caetano changed the regime's tone but not its core, and the war he would not end brought it down.
Salazar lived until July 1970; according to many accounts those around him never told him he was no longer in charge.

cards.title: 25 avril 1974

events.l: « Grândola, Vila Morena » à la radio : le signal
Caetano se rend au Largo do Carmo

cards.text: Le 25 avril 1974, de jeunes officiers du Mouvement des forces armées (MFA) renversèrent le régime presque sans effusion de sang. Des foules envahirent les rues et glissèrent des œillets dans les fusils des soldats : la révolution des Œillets.

deep.x: The Armed Forces Movement (MFA) began among captains tired of endless war, frozen careers and a regime with no way out. They planned the coup in secret and used radio songs as signals.
The day

Captain Salgueiro Maia led a column from the cavalry school in Santarém to Lisbon's Terreiro do Paço, then surrounded the Carmo barracks, where Caetano had taken refuge. Despite radio appeals to stay home, crowds poured into the streets to support the soldiers. That evening Caetano handed power to General Spínola.
Carnations

A restaurant worker, Celeste Caeiro, had carnations left over from a cancelled celebration. She gave one to a soldier, who put it in his rifle barrel; others copied, and the red carnation became the symbol of the revolution.
The only deaths came when DGS agents fired on the crowd outside their Lisbon headquarters. Political prisoners were freed from Caxias and Peniche days later.
These "three Ds" summed up the MFA's programme.
A coup by soldiers became a revolution because the people joined in.
25 April is a national holiday, Dia da Liberdade, and every year people still march down Lisbon's Avenida da Liberdade with red carnations.

cards.title: Décolonisation
cards.text: Après la révolution, le Portugal reconnut l'indépendance de la Guinée-Bissau (1974), du Mozambique, du Cap-Vert, de São Tomé-et-Príncipe et de l'Angola (1975). Environ un demi-million de « retornados » arrivèrent au Portugal.

deep.x: The MFA wanted to end the wars quickly, and the liberation movements wanted full independence, not the federation Spínola had imagined. Within about 18 months every African colony was independent.
Angola's tragedy

In Angola three rival movements fought each other as independence approached, each backed by foreign powers. The civil war that followed lasted, with pauses, until 2002. Mozambique also suffered a long civil war (1977–92).
The retornados

Hundreds of thousands of Portuguese settlers fled, many with only a suitcase. An emergency airlift in 1975 brought many home. They often arrived in a country they barely knew, sometimes facing suspicion, and were housed in hotels, camps and with relatives.
Timor and Macau
East Timor was invaded by Indonesia in December 1975; it won independence only in 2002 after a long struggle that Portugal championed. Macau was handed to China in 1999, ending the Portuguese empire.
Decolonisation was fast and chaotic, and its human costs fell on Africans and on returning Portuguese alike.
Portuguese is now an official language in nine countries, and the CPLP links them as a community.

cards.title: Construire la démocratie

events.l: Constitution et élection du premier président

cards.text: Après une période agitée (PREC), la Constitution de 1976 établit une république démocratique. Élections libres, presse libre et démocratie locale s'enracinèrent.

deep.x: The 19 months after the revolution are known as the **PREC** (Processo Revolucionário em Curso). Parties of every kind appeared, banks and big industries were nationalised, and in the Alentejo farm workers occupied large estates.
Hot summer

In 1975 the country was split. Communists and parts of the military pushed for a revolutionary state, while moderate parties, the Church and much of the north resisted; party offices were burned. On 25 November 1975 moderate officers stopped a radical military uprising, and the path to parliamentary democracy was secured.
The first free votes
The election of 25 April 1975 had the highest turnout in Portugal's history. The Socialists of Mário Soares came first, ahead of the Popular Democrats; the Communists got about 12%.
Settling down
The 1982 revision abolished the military Council of the Revolution, putting the armed forces fully under civilian control. Two IMF programmes (1977 and 1983) dealt with debts left by the upheaval.
Portugal's democracy emerged from a revolution that was turbulent but, compared with many, remarkably peaceful.

deep.w: The revolution was over on 25 April 1974
deep.r: The struggle over what kind of democracy lasted until at least late 1975

cards.title: Rejoindre l'Europe
cards.text: Le Portugal a rejoint la Communauté économique européenne le 1er janvier 1986, en même temps que l'Espagne. Les fonds européens ont aidé à construire routes, écoles et hôpitaux ; le Portugal a adopté l'euro en 1999 (pièces et billets en 2002).

deep.x: For Mário Soares, joining the European Community was the way to anchor democracy and modernise the economy. Portugal applied in 1977. After long negotiations the treaty was signed at the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon on 12 June 1985, and Portugal joined, with Spain, on 1 January 1986.
What changed

Billions of euros in structural and cohesion funds paid for motorways, bridges, sewers, schools and training. Farmers and fishermen had to adapt to European rules and competition. Portugal grew fast in the late 1980s and 1990s.
The euro
Portugal joined the euro at its launch in 1999. When notes and coins arrived in 2002, people converted every price in their heads.
1 euro = 200.482 escudos

x: A coffee at 100 escudos

deep.x: Europe gave Portugal money, markets and a democratic anchor, and in return Portugal had to compete in a much larger game.
Portugal has held the rotating presidency of the EU Council four times; the 2007 Lisbon Treaty, signed in the Jerónimos Monastery, still sets out how the EU works.

cards.title: L'Expo '98 et le Portugal moderne
cards.text: L'Expo '98 à Lisbonne a transformé le front de mer est et présenté un pays moderne. Depuis, le Portugal a connu des crises (plan de sauvetage de 2011) et est devenu une grande destination touristique et technologique.

deep.x: Expo '98 ran from May to September 1998 on the theme of the oceans, marking 500 years since Vasco da Gama reached India by sea. It turned a run-down industrial area of oil depots and a slaughterhouse in eastern Lisbon into the Parque das Nações.
Crisis and recovery

After 2008, high debt and weak growth caught up with Portugal. In 2011 it needed a €78 billion bailout from the EU and IMF (the "troika"), with deep cuts, tax rises and unemployment peaking around 17% in 2013. Many young people emigrated. Portugal exited the programme in 2014.
A new image

x: Tourism boomed, especially in Lisbon, Porto and the Algarve
The Web Summit moved to Lisbon in 2016, and start-ups followed
Portugal won Euro 2016, and António Guterres became UN Secretary-General in 2017
Housing costs rose sharply, a major political issue today

deep.x: In a generation, Portugal went from a closed, poor dictatorship to an open European democracy, with booms and busts along the way.
The Vasco da Gama Bridge, with its viaducts, is about 17 km long; it was the longest in Europe when it opened in 1998.

quiz.q: Qu'est-ce qui a donné à la radio le signal de la révolution du 25 avril 1974 ?
quiz.explain: La chanson de Zeca Afonso.

quiz.q: Quand le Portugal a-t-il rejoint la Communauté économique européenne ?
quiz.explain: En même temps que l'Espagne.

quiz.q: Quel général a dit célèbrement « Obviamente, demito-o ! » ?
quiz.explain: Pendant la campagne électorale de 1958.

lessons.title: Comment le Portugal est gouverné
lessons.summary: La Constitution, le président, le Parlement, le gouvernement, les tribunaux, les régions et le pouvoir local.

cards.title: La Constitution de 1976

deep.x: The Constituent Assembly elected on 25 April 1975 spent almost a year drafting the text amid the turmoil of the revolution. The result is long and detailed, with about 300 articles, and gives a large place to social rights such as health, education, housing and work.
What it contains

x: Freedoms of expression, assembly, religion and the right to strike
A ban on the death penalty and on life imprisonment
A national health service that is universal and tends to be free, and free compulsory schooling
Principles that no revision may remove, such as the republican form of government, universal suffrage and the separation of Church and State

deep.x: How it changes

The Assembly of the Republic may revise the Constitution five years after the last revision, or at any time if four-fifths of MPs agree to open the process. Each change needs a two-thirds majority, and the President cannot veto a revision.

x: 230 MPs
two-thirds needed
at least 154 votes to change the text

deep.w: The death penalty was abolished in 1976
deep.r: Portugal abolished it for civil crimes in 1867, among the first countries; the Constitution confirmed the ban

deep.x: The 1976 Constitution is the rulebook that every law, government and court in Portugal must obey.

cards.text:
La Constitution du Portugal a été approuvée le 2 avril 1976 par une assemblée élue un an après la révolution.

Elle définit le Portugal comme une république démocratique fondée sur la dignité humaine, l'État de droit et la séparation des pouvoirs. Elle a été révisée sept fois et reste la loi suprême.

cards.title: Le président

items: Veto sur les lois, dissolution du Parlement

deep.x: Portugal's system is often called **semi-presidential**: power is shared between a directly elected President and a Government that answers to parliament. In practice the Prime Minister leads day-to-day policy, while the President's power lies in a few strong but rarely used tools and in public influence.
The veto

When the Assembly sends a law, the President has 20 days to sign it or veto it, or 8 days to ask the Constitutional Court to check it. The Assembly can override a political veto by confirming the law with an absolute majority of MPs, or two-thirds for some kinds of law. A veto of a government decree is final.

x: 230 MPs
absolute majority = more than half
116 votes override a veto

deep.x: Dissolution

The President can dissolve the Assembly and call early elections, but not in the six months after it was elected, nor in the last six months of the presidential term, nor during a state of emergency. Because it is so drastic, it is nicknamed the "atomic bomb"; it was used three times between 2021 and 2025.
Elections

Candidates must be Portuguese citizens by origin, aged at least 35, and nominated by 7,500 to 15,000 voters, not by parties. To win in the first round a candidate needs more than half of the valid votes; otherwise the top two meet in a run-off three weeks later.
Every President elected since 1976 has gone on to win a second term.
The President rarely governs but holds the keys: who becomes Prime Minister and when the people vote again.

cards.text:
Le président de la République est le chef de l'État, élu directement par le peuple pour cinq ans et limité à deux mandats consécutifs.

Le rôle est surtout celui d'un arbitre. Le président ne dirige pas le gouvernement mais nomme le Premier ministre, peut opposer son veto aux lois et peut dissoudre le Parlement.

cards.title: L'Assemblée de la République

deep.x: What MPs do

x: Pass laws on almost every subject, including all laws on rights, elections and crimes
Approve the State Budget each year, usually in the autumn
Question ministers and the Prime Minister in regular debates and committees
Elect, by two-thirds, 10 of the 13 Constitutional Court judges and the Ombudsman

deep.x: Where MPs come from

The country is divided into 22 constituencies: the 18 mainland districts, the Azores, Madeira, and two for Portuguese living abroad, one for Europe and one for the rest of the world, each electing two MPs. The other seats are shared according to the number of registered voters, so Lisbon elects 48 MPs and Portalegre just 2.
Who can sit

Any voter can stand, but only on the list of a party or coalition; independents can appear on those lists. Since 2019, lists must include at least 40% of each sex. The Assembly is led by its own President, the second-highest office of the state after the President of the Republic.
The São Bento Palace was the Monastery of São Bento da Saúde until religious orders were abolished in 1834; parliament has met there ever since.
The Assembly is where the people's vote turns into laws, budgets and the rise and fall of governments.

cards.text:
L'Assemblée de la République est le parlement du Portugal, une chambre unique de 230 membres élus pour quatre ans.

Elle fait les lois, vote le budget, peut renverser le gouvernement et élit des responsables clés. Elle siège au palais de São Bento à Lisbonne, ancien monastère bénédictin.

cards.title: La méthode d'Hondt
example: Plus grands quotients : A 10 000, B 8 000, A 5 000, B 4 000, A 3 333
A obtient 3 sièges, B 2, C aucun

deep.x: How it works

Each list's votes are divided by 1, 2, 3 and so on. The seats go, one at a time, to the largest numbers in the whole table until all are filled. In effect, each new seat goes to the list that would have the most votes per seat after winning it.
Big and small constituencies

There is no legal minimum share of the vote, but constituency size matters a lot. In Lisbon, with 48 seats, a party can win a seat with around 2% of the vote. In a district with only 2 or 3 seats it may need 20% or more. That is why smaller parties win most of their MPs in Lisbon, Porto and Setúbal.
Rough threshold for one seat ≈ 100% ÷ (seats + 1)

x: Portalegre, 2 seats
Seat 1 to A; then B's 35 beats A's 20

deep.x: Strengths and criticisms
Proposals for reform, such as a national top-up constituency or letting voters choose candidates within lists, come up regularly but have not been adopted.
Portugal also uses d'Hondt for town councils, parish assemblies and its 21 seats in the European Parliament.
d'Hondt shares seats in proportion to votes, but its rounding favours larger parties, most of all where seats are few.

cards.text:
Les sièges sont répartis à la proportionnelle : les partis obtiennent des sièges à peu près en proportion de leurs voix.

Le Portugal utilise la méthode d'Hondt, conçue par le juriste belge Victor d'Hondt en 1878. Dans chaque circonscription, les électeurs choisissent une liste de parti, non des candidats individuels.

cards.title: Gouvernement et Premier ministre

deep.x: After an election, the President meets every party that won seats and then appoints as Prime Minister the person most likely to have parliament's support, usually the leader of the largest party or coalition. The Prime Minister proposes the ministers, whom the President then appoints.
Facing parliament

Within ten days, the new Government presents its programme to the Assembly. It does not need a vote of approval: it falls only if an absolute majority of MPs, 116, votes a motion of rejection. This rule lets minority governments take office, which has happened often since 1976.
How a government ends

x: A general election and a new Assembly
The Prime Minister's resignation or death
A censure motion passed by an absolute majority, or a lost confidence vote
Dismissal by the President, allowed only to protect the regular functioning of democratic institutions

deep.x: How it works inside

The Council of Ministers, all the ministers chaired by the Prime Minister, meets weekly to approve decree-laws and bills to send to parliament. The Prime Minister's official residence is a mansion behind the parliament building in São Bento.
Single-party absolute majorities are rare: they happened only in the elections of 1987, 1991, 2005 and 2022.
In Portugal a government does not need parliament's approval to start, only to avoid a majority voting against it.

cards.text:
Le gouvernement dirige le pays au quotidien : il propose le budget, dirige l'administration et peut prendre des décrets-lois.

Il est dirigé par le Premier ministre, nommé par le président au vu des résultats électoraux. Un gouvernement ne survit que tant que le Parlement ne le rejette ni ne le censure.

cards.title: La Cour constitutionnelle

deep.x: How judges are chosen

Ten judges are elected by the Assembly with a two-thirds majority, which in practice requires agreement between the largest parties. These ten then co-opt the remaining three. At least six must be career judges from other courts; the rest are legal experts, often law professors.
How a law reaches the Court

items: Gaps: a law that is missing

deep.x: If the Court finds a law unconstitutional before it is signed, the President must veto it. Once a rule is struck down with general binding force, it stops applying everywhere. Any ordinary court must also refuse to apply a rule it considers unconstitutional, and the case can then go to the Constitutional Court on appeal.
Between 2012 and 2014, for example, the Court struck down several budget measures, including cuts to public-sector holiday and Christmas pay, ruling that they treated groups unequally.
Other guardians

Prosecutions are led by the Public Prosecution Service, which is independent of the Government and headed by the Attorney General, appointed by the President on the Government's proposal for six years.

deep.w: The Constitutional Court hears every kind of appeal
deep.r: It decides only constitutional questions; ordinary cases end at the Supreme Court

deep.x: In Portugal no law is safe until it fits the Constitution, and 13 judges have the last word on that.

cards.text:
La Cour constitutionnelle décide si les lois respectent la Constitution et peut les annuler. Créée par la révision de 1982, elle compte 13 juges exerçant un seul mandat de neuf ans.

À ses côtés, des tribunaux indépendants, des procureurs, un Médiateur et une Cour des comptes surveillent les autres pouvoirs.

cards.title: Açores et Madère

deep.x: Autonomy answered old grievances: islanders had long felt neglected by Lisbon, and in 1975 small independence movements briefly appeared in both archipelagos. The Constitution gave them self-government within the Portuguese state, and their autonomy is among the principles no revision may remove.
What they control

x: Their own laws on matters such as health, education, transport, tourism, fisheries and farming
Most taxes raised in the region, with the power to lower some rates within limits
Their own flags, anthems and regional holidays

deep.x: The Representative of the Republic

The President appoints a Representative of the Republic for each region, who signs or vetoes regional laws and can send them to the Constitutional Court. The Representative also appoints the President of the Regional Government in light of the regional election results, much as the President of the Republic does with the Prime Minister.
Why not the mainland?

The Constitution also foresees administrative regions on the mainland, but in a 1998 referendum about 64% voted against creating eight of them. Turnout was under 50%, so the result was not binding, but no regions have been created since. Mainland planning is coordinated by five regional development commissions, the CCDRs.
The Azores spread their institutions across islands: the regional parliament sits in Horta, on Faial, while the regional government is based in Ponta Delgada, on São Miguel.
Autonomy lets the islands run most of their own affairs while remaining fully part of Portugal.

cards.text:
Les Açores et Madère sont des régions autonomes, statut créé par la Constitution de 1976 en raison de leur éloignement de Lisbonne et de leur identité insulaire.

Chacune a sa propre assemblée élue et son gouvernement régional, qui légifèrent sur de nombreuses questions locales. Défense, politique étrangère et justice restent à l'État national.

cards.title: Communes et paroisses

deep.x: The municipality

Each municipality has two bodies, both elected every four years. The Câmara Municipal is the executive; it is led by its president, the mayor, who is the first name on the most-voted list. The Assembleia Municipal debates and approves the budget and holds the Câmara to account; it also includes the presidents of all the parish councils.
The parish

Parishes are the level closest to citizens. They look after local paths and green spaces, issue some certificates, run markets and support schools and older people. In 2013 their number was cut from about 4,260 to about 3,090 by merging many rural parishes, and some of those mergers were reversed before the 2025 local elections.
Rules and money

x: Mayors may serve at most three consecutive terms in the same municipality
Groups of citizens can run independent lists in local elections, unlike in national ones
Councils are funded by local taxes such as the property tax (IMI), a share of state taxes and EU funds
Since 2019 many tasks in education, health and social support have been transferred from the state to the municipalities

deep.x: Corvo, in the Azores, is Portugal's smallest municipality and the only one with no parish at all.
Local power in Portugal runs from big-city mayors to parish councils that know every street by name.

cards.text:
Le pouvoir local compte deux niveaux : 308 communes, les concelhos, et en dessous plus de 3 000 paroisses, les freguesias.

Chacune a des organes élus qui gèrent les services locaux : routes, écoles, eau, déchets et culture. Maires et présidents de paroisse sont souvent les politiciens que les gens connaissent le mieux.

cards.title: Élections et vote

deep.x: Election day

Voting takes place on a Sunday, usually in schools. The day before is a "day of reflection": campaigning stops, and opinion polls cannot be published until voting ends. Ballot papers list the parties with their names and symbols, and voters mark a cross.
Who runs elections

The National Elections Commission, the CNE, watches over fairness and equal treatment of candidates, while the Ministry of Internal Administration handles the logistics. Citizens are registered automatically when they get their Citizen Card. Anyone can also ask to vote early, a week before, at a polling place of their choice.
Referendums

A national referendum must be proposed by the Assembly or the Government, checked by the Constitutional Court and called by the President. It is binding only if more than half of registered voters take part, and none of the three held so far reached that level.
After the 2007 vote, parliament chose to legislate in line with the majority anyway.

deep.w: Voting is compulsory in Portugal
deep.r: The Constitution calls voting a civic duty, but there is no fine for not voting

deep.x: Portugal's elections are frequent, free and simple: a cross on a Sunday, counted in public that same night.

cards.text:
Les citoyens de 18 ans et plus votent aux élections nationales, présidentielles, locales, régionales et européennes, ainsi que lors de référendums occasionnels.

Les élections ont lieu le dimanche, supervisées par une commission indépendante, et les votes sont dépouillés publiquement dans chaque bureau de vote.

cards.title: Le Portugal dans l'UE

items.b: des ministres votent pour le Portugal

deep.x: Membership means that some decisions are taken jointly in Brussels, Strasbourg and Luxembourg rather than in Lisbon alone. Trade, competition rules, farming and fisheries policy, and for euro countries interest rates, are largely set at EU level. Health, schools, pensions and most taxes remain mainly national.
How Portugal takes part

Ministers vote in the Council of the EU, where many decisions use a qualified majority. The Assembly's European Affairs Committee scrutinises EU proposals, and Portuguese judges and officials work in all the institutions.

x: 27 countries
at least 15 states (55%)
representing 65% of EU citizens = qualified majority

deep.x: Portuguese at the top
José Manuel Durão Barroso was President of the European Commission from 2004 to 2014, and António Costa has chaired the European Council since December 2024.
Language and courts

Portuguese is one of the EU's 24 official languages, so every EU law is published in it and citizens can write to the institutions in Portuguese. Portuguese courts can ask the EU Court of Justice in Luxembourg how to interpret EU law, and its answer binds them.
European Parliament elections in Portugal use a single national constituency, unlike general elections with their 22.
EU membership adds a European layer to Portuguese democracy: some laws are made jointly, and Portuguese help make them.

cards.text:
Depuis 1986, le Portugal est membre de l'Union européenne et partage certaines décisions avec 26 autres pays.

Il élit 21 députés européens, envoie des ministres au Conseil et propose un commissaire. Là où les traités donnent compétence à l'UE, le droit européen prime sur le droit national.

quiz.q: Combien de sièges compte l'Assemblée de la République ?
quiz.explain: 230 députés sont élus dans 22 circonscriptions.

quiz.q: Pour combien de temps le président de la République est-il élu ?
quiz.explain: Jusqu'à deux mandats consécutifs de cinq ans.

quiz.q: Dans la méthode d'Hondt, les voix de chaque liste sont divisées par quoi ?
quiz.explain: Les plus grands quotients remportent les sièges.

quiz.q: Qui décide si une loi respecte la Constitution ?
quiz.explain: Ses 13 juges exercent un seul mandat de neuf ans.

quiz.q: Quelles deux régions ont leur propre parlement et gouvernement ?
quiz.explain: Ce sont des régions autonomes depuis 1976.

lessons.title: L'économie du Portugal
lessons.summary: De l'entrée dans l'UE et du plan de sauvetage au tourisme, aux exportations, aux renouvelables, aux start-ups et aux salaires.

cards.title: Une petite économie ouverte

items.l: de la production vient des services

deep.x: What the economy is made of

Services include shops, tourism, transport, property, finance and public services. Industry is smaller than in Germany or Czechia but strong in a few clusters: cars and parts, paper and pulp, cork, textiles and shoes, food and wine, and oil refining at Sines.
Wealth per person

GDP per person is roughly €27,000 a year, about 80% of the EU average once differences in prices are taken into account. That places Portugal in the lower half of the EU, and in recent years several Central European members, such as Czechia, Slovenia and Lithuania, have moved ahead of it.

x: GDP ~€285 billion
÷ ~10.7 million people
≈ €27,000 per person a year

deep.x: Open to the world

Exports of goods and services were about 30% of GDP around 2010 and close to half by the 2020s, one of the biggest changes in the economy's history. Spain is by far the largest customer, taking around a quarter of goods exports, followed by France, Germany and the United States.

deep.w: Portugal mainly lives off farming and fishing
deep.r: Farming and fishing make up only about 2% of output; services and industry produce almost everything

deep.x: Portugal is a small, service-heavy economy that lives more and more by selling to the rest of the world.

cards.text:
L'économie du Portugal produit environ 285 milliards d'euros de biens et services par an, moins de 2 % du total de l'UE. Les services comme le tourisme, le commerce et la finance dominent.

Les exportations équivalent désormais à près de la moitié du PIB, bien plus qu'autrefois, si bien que le pays dépend fortement des ventes à l'étranger.

cards.title: De l'entrée dans l'UE à l'euro

deep.x: The catch-up years

Between 1986 and 2000, GDP per person rose from just over half to roughly 70% of the then EU average, measured in purchasing power. Foreign investment arrived, such as the Autoeuropa car plant at Palmela, and EU funds paid for infrastructure and training. As markets prepared for the euro, interest rates fell sharply, making borrowing cheap for families, firms and the state.
Why growth stalled

x: China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and Central European countries joined the EU in 2004, competing in the low-cost textiles, shoes and assembly work Portugal relied on
Inside the euro, Portugal could no longer devalue its currency to make its goods cheaper abroad
Cheap credit flowed into housing, roads and consumption more than into productive firms
Wages rose faster than productivity, so firms lost competitiveness

deep.x: EU money

Over four decades Portugal has received well over €100 billion in EU funds, counting farm support. Since 2021 the Recovery and Resilience Plan, known as the PRR, adds about €22 billion in grants and loans for health, housing, digital and green projects.

deep.w: The euro caused the crisis on its own
deep.r: Economists point to a mix: cheap credit, weak productivity, new global competition and the 2008 financial crash

deep.x: EU entry lifted Portugal fast, but the euro's first decade showed that cheap money alone does not make an economy productive.

cards.text:
L'adhésion à la Communauté européenne en 1986 a ouvert les marchés et apporté d'importants fonds européens, et le Portugal a connu une forte croissance pendant environ 15 ans.

Après l'arrivée de l'euro en 1999, la croissance a fortement ralenti. Les années 2000 sont devenues une « décennie perdue » où l'économie a à peine progressé tandis que les dettes s'accumulaient.

cards.title: Sauvetage et reprise

deep.x: Why it happened

By early 2011 the interest rate on Portugal's ten-year bonds had climbed above 7%, after Greece and Ireland had already needed rescues. The minority government resigned in March 2011 when parliament rejected its new austerity package, and in April it requested help.

items.b: about a third of the loan

deep.x: What the programme involved

x: Cuts to public wages and pensions, and higher taxes
Privatisation of the electricity company EDP, the grid operator REN, the airports company ANA and the postal service CTT
Labour market changes, such as lower severance pay
Four public holidays suspended from 2013 to 2015, then restored in 2016

deep.x: The recovery

Exports, tourism and foreign investment led the rebound. In 2019 the state recorded its first budget surplus in the democratic era. After the dip of the Covid pandemic, surpluses returned in 2023 and 2024, and public debt fell from about 135% of GDP in 2020 to about 95% in 2024.

x: Debt ~€270 billion
GDP ~€285 billion

deep.x: Portugal repaid its IMF loans early, finishing in 2018, years ahead of schedule.
The bailout years were painful, but within a decade Portugal went from rescue case to one of the eurozone's fastest debt reducers.

cards.text:
En 2011, incapable d'emprunter sur les marchés à des taux abordables, le Portugal a demandé à l'UE et au FMI un prêt de sauvetage. Trois ans de coupes budgétaires, de hausses d'impôts et de réformes ont suivi.

L'économie s'est depuis redressée : le chômage a baissé, l'État a dégagé des excédents budgétaires plusieurs années et la dette publique est passée sous 100 % du PIB.

cards.title: Tourisme

deep.x: Who comes

The United Kingdom has long been the biggest foreign market, especially for the Algarve and Madeira. Spain, Germany and France follow, and American visitors have grown fastest in recent years, helped by new direct flights.
Where they go

Lisbon, the Algarve and Madeira dominate, while Porto and the North have grown fast since low-cost flights expanded in the 2000s and 2010s. Lisbon's Humberto Delgado airport handled over 35 million passengers in 2024 and is close to capacity; in 2024 the government chose Alcochete, across the Tagus, for a new airport.
Benefits and strains

Short-term rentals, known as alojamento local, spread fast in Lisbon and Porto from the 2010s. They helped restore run-down buildings but added to pressure on rents, and rules on new licences have been changed several times. Lisbon charges a tourist tax of €4 per person per night.

deep.w: Tourism is all about foreigners
deep.r: Portuguese residents account for roughly three in ten nights spent in tourist lodgings

deep.x: Tourism has become a pillar of Portugal's exports and jobs, and managing its side effects is now a central policy question.

cards.text:
Le tourisme est l'une des plus grandes industries du Portugal. Les visiteurs viennent pour les plages, les villes, la cuisine, le golf et l'histoire, et en 2024 les hébergements touristiques ont enregistré environ 31 millions de clients.

Les dépenses des visiteurs étrangers, environ 27 milliards d'euros par an, font du tourisme la première exportation du pays.

cards.title: Ce que vend le Portugal

items: Carburants de la raffinerie de Sines

deep.x: Cars

The Volkswagen Autoeuropa plant at Palmela, opened in 1995, is one of the country's largest exporters; it builds the T-Roc, almost all for export. Stellantis builds vans in Mangualde, and hundreds of suppliers make seats, tyres, wiring and glass for car plants across Europe.
Textiles and shoes

The north, from Guimarães and Barcelos to Felgueiras and São João da Madeira, has long been the heart of textiles, clothing and footwear. Hit hard by Asian competition in the 2000s, many firms survived by moving upmarket: technical fabrics, short production runs, fast delivery to European brands and their own shoe labels. Textile and clothing exports reach around €6 billion a year, and shoes about €2 billion.
Other strengths

x: Paper and pulp from eucalyptus plantations
Refined fuels from Galp's refinery at Sines, the only one left since Matosinhos closed in 2021
Moulds and plastics from Marinha Grande and Leiria
Food such as tomato paste, olive oil and tinned fish

deep.x: Portugal has become the EU's largest bicycle maker, with many factories around Águeda.
Behind the image of sun and cork, Portugal is an industrial exporter wired into European supply chains.

cards.text:
Les exportations de biens du Portugal sont plus variées qu'on ne le pense. Les voitures et composants arrivent en tête, suivis des machines, des carburants raffinés, des plastiques, du papier, des textiles et des chaussures.

La plupart vont vers d'autres pays de l'UE, surtout l'Espagne, les entreprises portugaises s'insérant dans les chaînes d'approvisionnement européennes.

cards.title: Le liège : un leader mondial

deep.x: An industry built on one tree

Portugal has roughly a third of the world's cork oak forests, mostly in the Alentejo and the Tagus valley, yet it processes even more cork than it grows, importing raw bark from Spain and North Africa. The industry is clustered around Santa Maria da Feira, south of Porto, where hundreds of firms turn bark into finished goods. Corticeira Amorim, founded in 1870, is the world's largest cork company.
From bark to bottle

The planks rest outdoors for months, are boiled to clean and soften them, then dried. Natural stoppers are punched from the thickest planks. Thinner cork and offcuts are ground and glued into "technical" stoppers for sparkling and everyday wines; champagne corks are agglomerated cork topped with natural discs.
Beyond the bottle

x: Floor and wall tiles that are warm, quiet and springy underfoot
Insulation boards for walls and roofs
Shoe soles, sports balls, gaskets and fashion items
Heat shields that protect rockets and spacecraft at launch

deep.x: In the 2000s, screw caps and plastic stoppers took a big share of the market. The industry answered by tackling cork taint, the musty smell that spoils some wines, and by promoting cork as natural and recyclable.
Expanded cork insulation needs no added glue: heating the granules with steam releases cork's own resin, which binds them together.
Portugal turned the bark of a tree into a high-tech export industry that uses every last scrap.

cards.text:
Le Portugal est le premier producteur et exportateur mondial de liège, en vendant environ 1,2 milliard d'euros à l'étranger chaque année.

La plupart devient des bouchons de vin, mais le liège sert aussi aux sols, à l'isolation, aux chaussures et même aux engins spatiaux. Rien n'est perdu : les chutes sont broyées en granulés et pressées en nouveaux produits.

cards.title: Le vin à l'export

deep.x: Who buys

items: France: a big buyer of port

deep.x: Portugal exports less wine by volume than Spain or Italy, but its average export price has been rising as more is sold bottled and under brand names. Shared language and emigrant communities help in markets such as Brazil, Angola and Canada.
Port: a regulated brand

Port is still among the most valuable Portuguese wines sold abroad, though sales volumes have slowly fallen since the 2000s as tastes changed. Its supply is tightly managed: each year the Douro's regulator, the IVDP, sets how much grape must may be fortified into port, and each vineyard gets a share according to a grading of its site, from A downwards.

x: Fermenting grape juice
add grape spirit (~77% alcohol)
sweet port of about 20%

deep.x: Growers and pressures

Most vineyards are small family plots, and many growers sell grapes to cooperative wineries or large firms. Costs are high on steep terraces where machines cannot work, and labour at harvest is scarce. In 2024 many Douro growers struggled to sell their grapes at a fair price as unsold wine piled up, and climate change is bringing hotter, drier summers and earlier harvests.
Wine tourism has become a business of its own: quintas in the Douro and Alentejo now earn a growing share of their income from visits, meals and rooms.
Portuguese wine's economic challenge is to earn more from every bottle rather than to make more bottles.

cards.text:
Le Portugal produit environ 7 millions d'hectolitres de vin par an, parmi les douze premiers producteurs mondiaux, et en exporte près d'un milliard d'euros.

Le porto reste le produit le plus connu, mais les vins de table rapportent désormais davantage à l'étranger au total. L'objectif de la filière est de vendre moins de vins bon marché en vrac et plus de bouteilles à prix élevé.

cards.title: Électricité renouvelable

deep.x: Where it comes from

Dams on northern rivers, built from the 1950s on, long made hydropower the backbone of the system; in wet years it supplies over a quarter of electricity, in droughts much less. From the 2000s wind farms spread along the ridges of the interior, and since about 2019 solar power has boomed, especially in the Alentejo, after auctions set record-low prices.
Quitting coal

Portugal was the fourth EU country to stop burning coal for electricity, after Belgium, Austria and Sweden. Natural gas plants and imports from Spain now fill the gaps when rain, wind and sun fall short.
Challenges

x: Sun and wind vary, so the grid needs storage: pumped-storage dams pump water uphill when power is cheap and release it later, and large batteries are arriving
Links with Spain, and through Spain to France, are limited; the Iberian blackout of 28 April 2025, which began in the Spanish grid, cut power across mainland Portugal for most of a day
Large solar farms, wind turbines and power lines sometimes face local opposition over land and landscape

deep.x: Off Viana do Castelo, WindFloat Atlantic was one of the world's first floating offshore wind farms: three large turbines on platforms anchored in water about 100 m deep.
Rain, wind and sun now power most of Portugal's homes and factories, and the next challenge is keeping that supply steady.

cards.text:
Le Portugal est l'un des leaders européens de l'électricité propre. En 2024, les renouvelables, surtout hydraulique, éolien et solaire, ont fourni environ 70 % de l'électricité consommée dans le pays.

Sa dernière centrale à charbon a fermé en 2021, et les gouvernements se sont fixé des objectifs encore plus élevés pour 2030.

cards.title: Start-ups et Web Summit

deep.x: The Web Summit

Founded in Dublin in 2009, the Web Summit moved to Lisbon in 2016, drawn by state support, the large venue at Parque das Nações and the city's appeal. A 2018 agreement with the government and the city keeps it in Lisbon until 2028 in exchange for about €11 million a year. It now draws around 70,000 people each November.
Home-grown unicorns

Most of these firms keep large engineering teams in Portugal even when their headquarters are in the United States or elsewhere. Their fortunes vary: Farfetch, founded by José Neves, ran into financial trouble and was bought by South Korea's Coupang in 2024.
Why here?

x: Engineers from strong universities such as Técnico in Lisbon, FEUP in Porto and the University of Minho, at lower salaries than in London or Berlin
Good English, a time zone close to London's, quality of life and safety
Visas and tax schemes for start-ups, tech workers and remote workers
Large international firms also run tech centres in Lisbon, Porto and Braga

deep.x: Limits

Start-ups still find less local venture capital than in bigger hubs, and rising housing costs in Lisbon and Porto worry workers. Tech remains a small part of total employment compared with tourism or industry.
Many Portuguese start-ups are founded with the US market in mind from day one, registering their company there while building the product in Portugal.
Lisbon's tech scene is real and growing, though still small next to tourism or industry.

cards.text:
Depuis le milieu des années 2010, Lisbonne et Porto sont devenues des bases prisées des start-ups tech et des télétravailleurs.

Le Web Summit, l'une des plus grandes conférences tech du monde, se tient à Lisbonne chaque novembre depuis 2016. Une poignée d'entreprises fondées par des Portugais sont devenues des « licornes » valorisées à plus d'un milliard de dollars.

cards.title: Salaires et productivité

deep.x: Fourteen payments

Most workers receive 14 payments a year: 12 normal months plus a holiday allowance, the subsídio de férias, usually paid before the summer, and a Christmas allowance, the subsídio de Natal. To compare with countries that pay 12 times a year, multiply by 14 and divide by 12.

x: €920 × 14 payments

deep.x: Productivity
Output per hour worked is roughly two-thirds of the EU average. According to the OECD, Portuguese workers put in more hours a year than Germans, about 1,650 against 1,350, yet produce less per hour.

v.unit: hours worked per worker a year

deep.x: Why the gap?

x: Very many small firms, which invest less in machines, technology and training
A historic education gap: in 2000 over 40% of young people left school early, while today it is under 10%, but many older workers had little schooling
Low investment per worker, especially after the 2011 crisis
A large share of jobs in labour-intensive sectors such as tourism, retail and construction

deep.x: Pay and people

Because the minimum wage has risen faster than average pay, the gap between them has narrowed. Many young graduates move abroad for higher salaries, while Portugal itself attracts immigrants, who now make up more than a tenth of residents.

deep.w: The Portuguese earn less because they work less
deep.r: They work more hours than most Europeans; the gap is in output per hour

deep.x: In the long run pay follows productivity, so Portugal's wage question is above all about skills, investment and better-paid sectors.

cards.text:
Les salaires au Portugal figurent parmi les plus bas d'Europe occidentale. Le salaire minimum national a augmenté rapidement, à 920 € par mois en 2026, versé 14 fois par an.

Le problème de fond est la productivité : chaque heure travaillée produit bien moins de valeur que la moyenne de l'UE, ce qui limite la hausse possible des salaires.

lessons.title: Le Portugal et la mer
lessons.summary: Un petit pays face à un vaste océan : poisson, vagues, science, énergie et une côte qui change.

cards.title: Un petit pays, une immense mer

deep.x: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, 1982), a coastal state has full sovereignty over a territorial sea of 12 nautical miles, about 22 km. Beyond it, out to 200 nautical miles, about 370 km, lies the EEZ. There the state controls fish, oil, gas, minerals and energy, but other countries' ships and planes may pass freely.
Islands make the difference
Every island generates its own 200-mile zone. The Azores and Madeira lie scattered far out in the Atlantic, so each adds an enormous area of sea.

x: Land: about 92,000 km²
Sea (EEZ): about 1,700,000 km²
Ratio: about 18 to 1

deep.x: What it means

x: The navy and air force patrol it against illegal fishing and pollution
Portugal also coordinates search and rescue over an even larger part of the Atlantic, from Lisbon and Ponta Delgada
It holds potential resources, from fish to offshore wind and seabed minerals

deep.x: Most of this sea is very deep: beyond the narrow shelf, the floor drops to 3,000–5,000 m.

deep.w: Portugal is a small country
deep.r: On land it is mid-sized for Europe; counting its sea, it is one of the largest

deep.x: Counting its sea, Portugal is not a small country at all.

cards.text:
La zone économique exclusive (ZEE) du Portugal, la mer où il contrôle la pêche, l'énergie et les ressources du fond marin, couvre environ 1,7 million de km². C'est environ 18 fois sa superficie terrestre et l'une des plus grandes d'Europe.

Les eaux autour des Açores en représentent plus de la moitié.

cards.title: Revendiquer le fond marin

deep.x: Under UNCLOS, the continental shelf means the seabed and what lies beneath it, not the water above. A state automatically has rights over it out to 200 nm. Further out, usually up to 350 nm, it must show with geological and depth data that the sea floor is a natural prolongation of its territory.
Years of mapping

A special team, the EMEPC (Task Group for the Extension of the Continental Shelf), was set up in 2005 to gather the evidence. Using research ships, sonar and a remotely operated robot called Luso, able to dive to 6,000 m, it surveyed vast areas of the sea floor.
Under review

The UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, a panel of scientists, studies claims one at a time, and each review can take many years. Portugal has added updated data since 2009. Some areas overlap with seabed claimed by Spain to the south, near the Selvagens and the Canary Islands, which would have to be settled between the two countries.

x: Seabed if claim accepted ≈ 4,000,000 km²
Land ≈ 92,000 km²
About 40 times the land area

deep.x: The extended area would include seamounts and hydrothermal vents, among the least explored places on Earth.
Portugal is seeking rights to the seabed far beyond its coast through science and law rather than force.

cards.text:
Au-delà de 200 milles nautiques, un pays peut revendiquer des droits sur le fond marin s'il prouve qu'il prolonge naturellement son territoire. Le Portugal a soumis une telle demande à l'ONU en 2009.

Si elle est acceptée, elle ajouterait environ 2 millions de km² de fond marin, portant le total à environ 4 millions de km².

cards.title: Des eaux froides et riches

deep.x: In summer the Azores High to the west and low pressure over hot Iberia make north winds, the nortada, blow along the coast. Because of the Earth's rotation, moving water in the northern hemisphere is deflected to the right, so the surface layer drifts west, away from the shore. Deep water, cold and full of nutrients, wells up to take its place.
A food factory

Nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates fertilise microscopic algae, the phytoplankton. They feed tiny animals, the zooplankton, which feed sardines, mackerel and anchovies, and in turn bigger fish, dolphins, seabirds and people. Upwelling coasts cover a tiny share of the world's ocean but supply a large share of the world's fish catch.
Why the south is warmer

The Algarve's south coast faces away from the north winds and is sheltered, so upwelling there is weaker. Its beaches are often several degrees warmer than those near Lisbon or in the Minho. On the west coast, a sudden cold spell in the water usually means the nortada has been blowing hard for days.
Iberia's upwelling is the northern end of the Canary Current system, one of the four great coastal upwelling regions of the world, along with those off California, Peru and south-west Africa.
Portugal's cold summer sea is the price of its rich fishing grounds.

cards.text:
Les nageurs de la côte ouest du Portugal savent que l'Atlantique est froid même en août. La raison est la remontée d'eaux profondes : en été, les vents du nord repoussent l'eau de surface loin de la côte, et l'eau froide des profondeurs monte la remplacer.

Cette eau profonde est pleine de nutriments, ce qui explique la richesse en poissons de ces mers.

cards.title: Une nation de mangeurs de poisson

viz.unit: kg par personne et par an (approx.)

deep.x: Fishing has shaped coastal towns from Caminha to Vila Real de Santo António. Most of the fleet's several thousand vessels are under 12 m long and fish close to shore with nets, lines and traps. Larger trawlers and purse-seiners work further out. Fishing is now a small share of jobs, but it keeps harbours, markets and restaurants alive along the whole coast.
The sardine crisis

Sardines are the symbol of the summer festivals, but the stock off Iberia fell sharply in the 2010s. Portugal and Spain cut catches hard, at times closing the fishery for months. The stock then recovered and catches were raised again, though scientists keep a close watch, because sardine numbers swing with ocean conditions.
From boat to plate

x: Fresh fish must first be sold at public auctions (lotas) run by the state company Docapesca
Canneries in Matosinhos, Peniche and Olhão turn sardines, mackerel and tuna into tins, a tradition from the 1800s
Portugal still imports much of the fish it eats, including almost all of its cod

deep.x: Portuguese tinned fish has become a gourmet export, sold in brightly decorated tins in specialist shops around the world.
Fish is part of Portuguese identity, and keeping it on the table means fishing only what the sea can replace.

cards.text:
Les Portugais mangent plus de poisson et de fruits de mer par habitant que n'importe qui d'autre dans l'UE, environ 57 kg par an, plus de deux fois la moyenne européenne.

Sardines grillées, poulpe, chinchard et palourdes sont des plats du quotidien, débarqués par une flotte composée surtout de petits bateaux.

cards.title: L'histoire de la morue

events.l: Début de la campagne de la morue
La Flotte blanche à son apogée

deep.x: Salted, dried cod keeps for months without a fridge, so it suited a seafaring Catholic country with many meatless fast days. Portuguese fishermen were working the Grand Banks off Newfoundland soon after 1500, using salt from Aveiro and the Tagus.
The White Fleet

Under the Estado Novo, a state-organised "cod campaign" from 1934 aimed to make Portugal self-sufficient. Each spring the White Fleet, white-painted sailing ships and trawlers, left for months on the Grand Banks and off Greenland. Men fished alone from small flat-bottomed boats called dories, with hand lines, often in fog and icy water, and many never came home.
The hospital ship Gil Eannes sailed with them; it is now a museum in Viana do Castelo.
Why it ended

In 1977 Canada extended its fishing limits to 200 nm, closing most of the Grand Banks to foreign fleets. Overfishing then caused the collapse of Newfoundland cod, and Canada closed that fishery in 1992. Portugal turned to imports, mainly from Norway, where cod is now often salted especially for the Portuguese market.

deep.w: Bacalhau is a Portuguese fish
deep.r: It is Atlantic cod from cold northern seas; Portugal has almost no cod of its own and imports nearly all of it

deep.x: Bacalhau is a taste of history: a fish from distant northern seas that became the heart of Portuguese cooking.

cards.text:
La morue ne vit pas dans les eaux portugaises, pourtant le bacalhau est le plat national. Pendant des siècles, les navires portugais ont gagné Terre-Neuve et le Groenland pour la pêcher et la saler.

Aujourd'hui, la plus grande partie vient de Norvège et d'Islande, et on la mange toujours salée, dessalée et cuisinée de centaines de façons.

cards.title: Les vagues géantes de Nazaré

steps: Le canyon garde les vagues rapides
Les vagues se rejoignent à Praia do Norte

deep.x: Normally, as waves approach a coast, the shallow continental shelf slows them and drains their energy. At Nazaré, the canyon, well over 150 km long, cuts straight through the shelf to within about a kilometre of the shore, so waves arrive with much of their power intact.
How the canyon builds waves

Waves travelling over the deep canyon keep their speed, while those crossing the shallow shelf on either side slow down and bend. The two sets meet near the beach and add together into a towering peak, and local currents can steepen them further.
Records

Big-wave surfers at Nazaré use tow-in surfing: a jet-ski pulls them onto the wave, because waves this fast are almost impossible to paddle into. A second jet-ski waits to rescue them after a fall. The best season is roughly October to March, when deep Atlantic storms send long swells.
Watching

The red lighthouse at the Fort of São Miguel Arcanjo, on the headland, is the classic viewpoint, and crowds gather there on big days. Before surfers came, Nazaré was known as a fishing town, where boats were hauled up the beach by oxen.

deep.w: Nazaré's waves are caused by earthquakes or tsunamis
deep.r: They are ordinary storm swells, focused and amplified by the shape of the seabed

deep.x: At Nazaré, the shape of the seabed turns ordinary Atlantic swells into giants.

cards.text:
La Praia do Norte de Nazaré produit certaines des plus grosses vagues surfables de la planète, plus de 20 m les meilleurs jours d'hiver.

Le secret est sous l'eau : le canyon de Nazaré, une gorge du fond marin profonde d'environ 5 000 m, court presque jusqu'à la plage et concentre l'énergie des houles atlantiques.

cards.title: Science et protection de l'océan

items: Recherche sur la pêche et le climat

deep.x: Ocean science in Portugal has royal roots. King Carlos I, who reigned from 1889 to 1908, was a keen oceanographer who led research cruises off the coast on his yachts, collecting deep-sea fish and studying the sea. Today institutes such as IPMA, CIIMAR in Matosinhos and Okeanos at the University of the Azores carry on the work.
Life without sunlight

In the 1990s scientists found hydrothermal vents on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge south-west of the Azores, with names like Lucky Strike, Menez Gwen and Rainbow. Seawater seeps into hot rock, heats to over 300 °C and gushes out loaded with minerals. Bacteria use these chemicals for energy, and shrimps, mussels and crabs live on the bacteria, in a food web that runs without sunlight.
Protecting the sea
In the Azores network, about half of the protected area is closed to all fishing. Lisbon co-hosted the UN Ocean Conference with Kenya in 2022.
Some vents and seamounts hold metal-rich deposits, and many scientists warn that mining them could destroy ecosystems before they are understood.
Some vent microbes and animals survive temperatures and chemicals that would kill almost any other life, and are studied for clues to how life began.
Portugal's waters hold some of the Atlantic's strangest life, and the country now protects a growing share of them.

cards.text:
L'immense mer du Portugal en fait un lieu important pour la recherche océanique. Des sources chaudes sous-marines près des Açores, des canyons profonds et des monts sous-marins abritent une vie qu'on ne trouve nulle part ailleurs.

En 2024, les Açores ont créé le plus grand réseau d'aires marines protégées de l'Atlantique Nord, couvrant 30 % de leur mer.

cards.title: Ports et câbles

deep.x: Sines was a small fishing town until the 1970s, when the state built a large port and industrial complex there. Its great advantage is deep water close to shore, so even the largest ships can dock. A container terminal opened in 2004, and its gas terminal, receiving liquefied gas by ship, became more important to Europe after 2022.
Transshipment

Many containers at Sines are only changing ships. Giant vessels drop boxes that smaller ships carry on to other ports in Europe, Africa and the Mediterranean. This makes Sines Portugal's busiest container port and a link in global trade routes.
The cable coast

Almost all intercontinental internet traffic travels through undersea fibre-optic cables. Portugal's position makes it a natural landing point. The EllaLink cable, opened in 2021, links Sines directly with Fortaleza in Brazil, and other cables reach Africa and the United States. Large data centres are being built at Sines to use these links.

items: Cables to Africa and the US

deep.x: Sines is the birthplace of Vasco da Gama, whose statue stands by the castle overlooking the port.

deep.w: Ships are old-fashioned in the internet age
deep.r: About 80% of world trade by volume still travels by sea, and the internet itself runs mostly on undersea cables

deep.x: Portugal's coast is a crossroads for both ships and data, linking Europe to the Atlantic world.

cards.text:
Le Portugal se trouve près de certaines des routes maritimes les plus fréquentées du monde, entre l'Europe, l'Afrique et les Amériques. Son plus grand port, Sines, est un pôle en eau profonde pour les porte-conteneurs et l'énergie.

Sous la mer courent des câbles à fibre optique reliant l'Europe à l'Afrique et aux Amériques, plusieurs atterrissant sur la côte portugaise.

cards.title: Vent et vagues en mer

deep.x: WindFloat Atlantic has three turbines of about 8.4 MW each, 25 MW in total, about 20 km off the coast where the sea is around 100 m deep. Each stands on a triangular floating platform held in place by chains and anchors. The platforms were assembled in port and towed out to sea, avoiding costly work offshore.
Why floating

Fixed turbines on foundations work in water up to about 50–60 m deep, as across much of the North Sea. Off Portugal, such depths are often only a few kilometres from shore. Floating platforms can go into deep water, where winds are strong and steady.
Plans and doubts

The government has mapped areas for offshore wind off Viana do Castelo, Leixões, Figueira da Foz, Ericeira and Sines, and plans auctions for several gigawatts. Fishermen worry about losing fishing grounds, and floating wind still costs more than wind on land, so the timetable remains uncertain.
Wave power

The Aguçadoura wave farm near Póvoa de Varzim was the world's first multi-machine wave farm, in 2008, but it ran only briefly because of technical and financial problems. Waves remain a promising but hard-to-harvest resource.
Pico, in the Azores, had one of the world's first wave power plants connected to a grid, which worked on and off from 1999 until 2018.
Deep water close to shore turned a handicap into an opportunity: Portugal learned to float its wind turbines.

cards.text:
Le plateau continental du Portugal est étroit, si bien que le fond marin plonge brutalement loin de la côte. Cela exclut les éoliennes offshore fixes ordinaires presque partout.

Le Portugal a donc été pionnier de l'éolien flottant : le parc WindFloat Atlantic au large de Viana do Castelo, ouvert en 2020, fut le premier de son genre en Europe continentale.

cards.title: Niveau de la mer et côte

items: Montée du niveau de la mer
Trop peu de sable des fleuves

deep.x: Sand on the west coast moves mostly from north to south, pushed by waves that usually arrive from the north-west. This longshore drift is fed by rivers, especially the Douro. Dams built in the 20th century trapped much of that sediment, and long jetties at ports such as Leixões and Aveiro block the flow further. Beaches to the south of them are starved of sand.
Sea level rising

Cascais has one of the oldest tide gauges in the world, recording since 1882. It shows sea level rising by about 20 cm since then, and the rate has increased in recent decades. Global projections for 2100 range from roughly 30 cm to about 1 m above recent levels, depending mainly on future greenhouse gas emissions.
Defend, adapt or retreat

x: **Groynes and seawalls**: rock barriers protect places like Espinho, but often push erosion further south
**Sand nourishment**: pumping sand from offshore or harbours onto beaches, as at Costa da Caparica
**Managed retreat**: removing buildings from the most exposed spots, as on some barrier islands of the Ria Formosa

deep.w: The coastline is fixed
deep.r: Coasts always move; the problem is that people have built right up to a shoreline that is now retreating

deep.x: Portugal's coast is retreating because the sea is rising and its sand supply has been cut, and living with it means giving the coast room.

cards.text:
De longs tronçons de la côte portugaise reculent, les plages et les dunes perdant du sable. Les barrages retiennent les sédiments que les fleuves apportaient autrefois, et les digues des ports bloquent la dérive naturelle du sable.

Le niveau de la mer monte aussi, si bien que les tempêtes pénètrent plus loin dans les terres. Des villes comme Espinho et Costa da Caparica dépensent beaucoup pour défendre leurs plages.

quiz.explain: Environ 18 fois sa superficie terrestre.

options: La fonte de la glace arctique
quiz.explain: Les vents du nord repoussent l'eau de surface vers le large.

quiz.q: Qu'est-ce qui rend les vagues de Nazaré si grosses ?
quiz.explain: Le canyon concentre l'énergie de la houle.

options: Le flottant est moins cher partout
